subject: Error Covariance Structure of Linear Multilevel Model for Change

messages.author: e43f78aad52dc683
messages.subject: Error Covariance Structure of Linear Multilevel Model for Change
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I tried to reproduce the examples in chapter 7 "Examining the Multilevel Model's Error Covariance Structure" of Singer/Wíllett "Applied Longitudinal Data Analysis". I want to run a linear multilevel model with a autoregressive error covariance matrix.
So far, I found some code for a multilevel model (http://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/63849_aa651d1340fd4a00ac17cffd0374a8ec.html), added a random slope and covariance matrix. Can you give me a hint which parameter in my code I have to focus on to impose a autoregressive covariance matrix? Is that possible with stan?
The data consists of 35 persons whose performance at a test is measured at four different time points. The multilevel model has a random intercept, random slope (time), and an interaction effect (time*cognitive skill).

Here you can find the code I used:

library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

opposites <- read.csv("opposites_pp.csv")

modelString =
  '
data {
  int<lower=0> Ni;
  int<lower=0> Nj;
  int<lower=1> cluster[Ni];
  real Y_ij[Ni];
  real X_1ij[Ni];
  real x2[Ni];
  real x3[Ni];
  vector[2] daw;
}

parameters {
  vector[2] beta_0;
 
  // Random effects
  vector[2] u_0j[Nj];
  //real u_1j[Nj];
  // Standard deviation of random effects
  real sigma_u0;
  real sigma_u1;

  // Population slope
  real beta_2;
  real beta_3;

  // Population standard deviation
  real<lower=0> sigma;

  //scaling
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho;
}

transformed parameters {
 
  // Varying intercepts
  real beta_0j[Nj];
   // Varying slopes
  real beta_1j[Nj];
  // Individual mean
  real mu[Ni];
  //covariance-matrix
  matrix[2,2] as;

  as[1,1] = square(sigma_u0);
  as[2,2] = square(sigma_u1);
  as[1,2] = sigma_u0*sigma_u1*rho;
  as[2,1] = as[1,2];


  // Varying intercepts definition
  for (j in 1:Nj) {
    beta_0j[j] = beta_0[1] + u_0j[j,1];
  }

  // Varying slopes definition
  for (j in 1:Nj) {
    beta_1j[j] = beta_0[2] + u_0j[j,2];
  }

  // Individual mean
  for (i in 1:Ni) {
    mu[i] = beta_0j[cluster[i]] + beta_1j[cluster[i]] * X_1ij[i] + beta_2*x2[i] + beta_3*x3[i];
  }
}

model {
  // Prior part of Bayesian inference
  // Flat prior for mu (no need to specify if non-informative)
  beta_0[1] ~ normal(0, 100);
  beta_0[2] ~ normal(0, 100);
 
  u_0j ~ multi_normal(daw, as);

  // Likelihood part of Bayesian inference
  // Outcome model N(mu, sigma^2) (use SD rather than Var)
  for (i in 1:Ni) {
    Y_ij[i] ~ normal(mu[i], sigma);   
  }
}
'

opposites$time_ccog <-  opposites$time*opposites$ccog

opposites_dat <- list(Ni = dim(opposites)[1],
                      Nj = 35,
                      Y_ij = opposites$opp,
                      cluster=opposites$id,
                      X_1ij = opposites$time,
                      x2 = opposites$ccog,
                      x3 = opposites$time_ccog,
                      daw=c(0,0))



stanDso <- stan_model(model_code=modelString)

fit <- sampling(object=stanDso, data = opposites_dat, warmup=200, iter = 1000, chains=4, verbose=T)

opp_results <- as.data.frame(summary(fit))
 



The data files can be found here: http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/examples/alda.htm

Thank you very much

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error Covariance Structure of Linear Multilevel Model for Change
parts:
What's an autoregressive covariance matrix?

If you have positive constrained paramters like scales, you
need to constrain them with <lower=0> so that the model's
support matches the constraints on the parameters.

You can vectorize these:

>
> // Varying slopes definition
> for (j in 1:Nj) {
> beta_1j[j] = beta_0[2] + u_0j[j,2];
> }

>
> // Individual mean
> for (i in 1:Ni) {
> mu[i] = beta_0j[cluster[i]] + beta_1j[cluster[i]] * X_1ij[i] + beta_2*x2[i] + beta_3*x3[i];
> }

mu = beta_0j[cluster] + beta_1j[cluster] .* X1ij + beta_2 * x2 + beta_3 * x3;

You just have to make sure everything's declared as a vector
or matrix rathe than array, e.g.,

> real beta_0j[Nj];

becomes

vector[Nj] beta_0j;

Then, the big time saver will be vectorizing this

as

Y_ij ~ normal(mu, sigma);

I'd be inclined to use a scaled Cholesky factor for
correlation matrices with an LKJ prior and an independent
prior on the scales rather than your covariance
structure. We describe that in the regression chapter of
the manual.

Not having any priors at all on the scales can be problematic
for inference, becuase it implies most of the mass is on
large values. If you have lots of data it should be OK.

A non-centered parameterization of the covariance structure
will also likely be a lot faster.

- Bob

P.S. Terminologically, priors and likelihoods are part of the model.
Computing posteriors, estimates, event probabilities, predictions,
etc. are inference.
